title: Scripture proves itself by innate notes of divinity — like creation or a classic author's genius
source_text: XXXIII. Praeterea hic observandum est, testimonia, quibus Scriptura sacra se divinam asserit, non esse quidem idonea & efficacia argumenta ad convincendos eos qui in dubium vocant Scripturae authoritatem; Et eatenus verum est Scripturam per Scripturam probari non posse. Sed tamen alio sensu Scriptura per Scripturam ipsam probari potest, quatenus Scripturae insunt multa divinitatis argumenta & notae quibus ipsa se veram & divinam indicat & asserit. Non secus ac caelum & terra probant & ostendunt suum authorem Deum esse, non simplici aliqua voce & testimonio, sed ex ipsa suae naturae praestantia, & potentiae ac sapientiae divinae vestigiis quae in illis notari possunt: aut ut aliquis liber Aristoteli & Ciceroni se vindicat, non ex solo titulo, sed ex ipsius doctrinae genio, acumine styli & differendi modo, qui ejusmodi est ut non possit nisi praestantibus illis ingeniis tribui. Ita enim Scripturae libri, seu stylum, seu res ipsas spectes, tam alte impressa habent sapientiae divinae vestigia, ut satis appareat illos divinitus inspiratos esse, & Deum habere authorem.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover here it is to be observed, that the testimonies by which sacred Scripture asserts itself divine are not indeed suitable and efficacious arguments for convincing those who call the authority of Scripture into doubt; And so far it is true that Scripture cannot be proved by Scripture. But yet in another sense Scripture can be proved by Scripture itself, inasmuch as there are in Scripture many arguments and notes of divinity by which it indicates and asserts itself true and divine. Not otherwise than heaven and earth prove and show that God is their author, not by some simple voice and testimony, but from the very excellence of their nature, and the vestiges of divine power and wisdom which can be noted in them: or as some book vindicates itself for Aristotle and Cicero, not from the title alone, but from the genius of its doctrine, the acuity of style and manner of discoursing, which is of such a kind that it cannot be attributed except to those outstanding minds. For so the books of Scripture, whether you look at style or at the things themselves, have so deeply impressed the vestiges of divine wisdom that it sufficiently appears that they were divinely inspired, and have God as author.
pass_b_english: Bare self-assertions in Scripture do not convince those who already doubt its authority — in that sense Scripture cannot prove Scripture.
Yet another sense holds: Scripture carries many innate notes of divinity by which it shows itself true and divine.
As heaven and earth prove God by excellence and wisdom's traces — not by a spoken certificate.
As a book claims Aristotle or Cicero by genius of doctrine and style, not by the title page alone.
Scripture's books likewise bear divine wisdom so deeply that inspiration and divine authorship appear.

choices.english: in another sense ... by Scripture itself
choices.why: Distinguish bare self-citation from innate marks.
rejected: Scripture never proves Scripture in any sense

choices.term: notae quibus ipsa se veram & divinam indicat
choices.english: notes by which it indicates itself true and divine
